1.title: Course Introduction, Exam Orientation and the Six Scenarios
1.text: Welcome to Module zero: Course Introduction, Exam Orientation and the Six Scenarios. This module covers exam orientation, the six scenarios and the course map. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. What the exam is: sixty scenario-based items, one hundred twenty minutes, a scaled score of seven hundred twenty to pass. The five domains, their weights and the thirty task statements behind them. The six scenarios (you meet four of them on exam day) and which domains each one tests. The ten decision rules that explain most correct answers. How the course is built and how to use it.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply. Throughout the course you follow Birchwood Supply, a fictional online retailer. Its support agent answers returns and billing questions, its research assistant writes market reports, and its engineers use Claude Code every day. Each module solves one problem of this company; the questions use the same style as the exam scenarios.

1.title: The Exam at a Glance
1.text: The Exam at a Glance. The figure shows this: The C C A R F exam at a glance: sixty items, one hundred twenty minutes, scaled score one hundred to one thousand with seven hundred twenty to pass, four of six scenarios, U S D one hundred twenty-five, valid twelve months.

1.title: The Exam at a Glance, continued
1.text: The Exam at a Glance, continued. Credential or code. Claude Architect to Foundations or C C A R F. Items. sixty, multiple choice and multiple response; each item says how many answers to select. Structure. four scenarios picked at random from a bank of six; the questions are framed by the scenario. Time. one hundred twenty minutes (about two minutes per item). Passing score. seven hundred twenty on a scaled range of one hundred to one thousand (criterion-referenced: you are measured against a fixed standard, not against other candidates). Fee. U S D one hundred twenty-five per attempt. Delivery. Proctored by Pearson V U E: online or at a test center; closed book.

1.title: The Exam at a Glance, continued
1.text: The Exam at a Glance, continued. Validity. twelve months; renewal on time is a free, non-proctored assessment; a lapsed credential needs the full exam again. Retakes. Wait fourteen days after the first failed attempt, thirty after the second, ninety after the third; at most four attempts in a rolling twelve months; limits are per exam. Score report. Pass or fail, the scaled score, and the percent correct per domain (the domain figures do not decide pass or fail).

1.title: The Exam at a Glance, continued
1.text: The Exam at a Glance, continued. Who can sit it. Exams are open to people who work at organizations in the Claude Partner Network, registering with a company email on the organization's listed domain; candidates must be eighteen or older with a government photo I D whose name matches the registration. People outside the network can take the free Anthropic Academy courses, which give completion certificates, not the credential. This course teaches the same knowledge to everyone. Exam tip: Item formats are not scored differently. For a multiple-response item the stem says how many to pick: read that number first, then choose exactly that many.

1.title: The Five Domains, continued
1.text: The Five Domains, continued. Out of scope (will not appear): fine-tuning or training models; A P I (application programming interface) authentication, billing or account management; programming-language specifics; deploying or hosting M C P servers; model internals, R L H F or Constitutional A I; embeddings and vector databases; computer use; vision; streaming and server-sent events; rate limits, quotas or pricing math; OAuth and key rotation; cloud-provider setup; benchmarking; prompt caching details; tokenization.

1.title: The Six Scenarios
1.text: The Six Scenarios. The figure shows this: The six scenarios and the domains they mostly test.

1.title: The Six Scenarios, continued
1.text: The Six Scenarios, continued. one. Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. What you build: Agent S D K (software development kit) agent with M C P tools get customer, lookup order, process refund, escalate to human; target eighty percent plus first-contact resolution and knowing when to escalate. Primary domains: D one, D two, D five. two. Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. What you build: Team use of Claude Code: slash commands, Claude dot M D, plan mode versus direct execution. Primary domains: D three, D five. three. Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. What you build: Coordinator with subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis, report generation; cited reports. Primary domains: D one, D two, D five.

2.title: The Six Scenarios, continued
2.text: The Six Scenarios, continued. four. Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude. What you build: Agent S D K tools to explore codebases, using Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob and M C P servers. Primary domains: D two, D three, D one. five. Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration. What you build: Automated code review, test generation and P R (pull request) feedback in C I; minimize false positives. Primary domains: D three, D four. six. Scenario: Structured Data Extraction. What you build: Extract data from unstructured documents, validate with Jason (Java Script Object Notation) schemas, handle edge cases. Primary domains: D four, D five. Exam tip: You will not know in advance which four scenarios you get, so study all six. Module fifteen walks through each one from the first requirement to the best architecture.

2.title: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward
2.text: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward. Most items present a problem seen in logs or production data and four plausible fixes. The best answer usually follows one of these rules. Learn them now; each later module shows them at work.

2.title: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward, continued
2.text: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward, continued. one. Rule: A hard business requirement needs programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates), because prompts have a non-zero failure rate. Typical wrong answers: Stronger system prompt wording, more few-shot examples. two. Rule: Find the root cause from the evidence given before choosing the fix (the logs usually name it). Typical wrong answers: Blaming a downstream agent that behaved correctly. three. Rule: Choose the proportionate first step: low effort, high leverage (better tool descriptions, explicit criteria, a few examples) before new infrastructure. Typical wrong answers: A separate classifier, a routing layer, fine-tuning.

2.title: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward, continued
2.text: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward, continued. four. Rule: Least privilege: each agent gets only the tools its role needs, plus a narrow shared tool for a frequent need. Typical wrong answers: Giving every agent every tool. five. Rule: Structured beats generic: structured errors, structured handoffs, claim-to-source mappings, case-fact blocks. Typical wrong answers: "Operation failed", free-text summaries. six. Rule: Self-reported confidence and sentiment are weak proxies for difficulty; use explicit criteria and calibrated, validated signals. Typical wrong answers: "Escalate when confidence less than seven", sentiment thresholds. seven. Rule: Independent review beats self-review; split big reviews into per-file passes plus an integration pass. Typical wrong answers: Asking the same session to double-check itself; a bigger context window.

2.title: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward, continued
2.text: Ten Decision Rules the Questions Reward, continued. eight. Rule: Match the A P I to the latency need: synchronous for blocking steps, batch for overnight work. Typical wrong answers: Batch for pre-merge checks. nine. Rule: Never suppress errors and never abort everything: return partial results with failure context and annotate gaps. Typical wrong answers: Empty result marked as success; kill the whole run on one timeout. ten. Rule: Context is a budget: isolate verbose work in subagents, persist key facts outside summaries, trim tool output. Typical wrong answers: Reading everything up front, relying on a long history. Exam tip: When two options both "work", prefer the one that is deterministic, specific, scoped and proportionate. Words like "always", "guarantee" and "must" in the requirement point to rule one.

2.title: The Technologies at a Glance
2.text: The Technologies at a Glance. The figure shows this: How the pieces fit: Claude A P I at the base, Agent S D K for building agents, Claude Code as the ready-made agent and C L I (command-line interface), and M C P connecting tools and data.

2.title: The Technologies at a Glance, continued
2.text: The Technologies at a Glance, continued. Claude A P I. What it is: The Messages A P I: send messages, define tools (tool use), steer with tool choice, read stop reason, cap output with max tokens, set a system prompt; Message Batches A P I for asynchronous bulk work. Exam focus: D one loops, D two tool choice, D four structured output and batches. Claude Agent S D K. What it is: The same agent loop that powers Claude Code, as a library: tools, subagents, hooks, sessions. Exam focus: D one, D two, D five. Claude Code. What it is: The coding agent and C L I: Claude dot M D, rules, skills, plan mode, M C P servers, dash p for scripts and C I. Exam focus: D three, D two.

2.title: The Technologies at a Glance, continued
2.text: The Technologies at a Glance, continued. M C P (Model Context Protocol). What it is: An open standard to connect tools (actions), resources (read-only content catalogs) and prompts to an agent. Exam focus: D two. Jason Schema or Pydantic. What it is: Describe and validate structured output. Exam focus: D four.

2.title: How to Use This Course
2.text: How to Use This Course. Order: read modules one to fourteen in order (they follow the guide's domains), then module fifteen (scenarios), sixteen (recap) and seventeen (exam technique). Each module has task statements, a case, tables, figures, Exam tips, six or more scenario questions with explanations, and a Quick Reference Card.

2.title: How to Use This Course, continued
2.text: How to Use This Course, continued. Hands-on practice matters. The guide recommends four exercises: (one) a multi-tool agent with escalation logic; (two) Claude Code configured for a team (Claude dot M D, rules, a skill, an M C P server); (three) a structured extraction pipeline with validation, retry and batches; (four) a multi-agent research pipeline with error propagation and provenance. Do at least the first two with real code. Product details change fast (tool names, flags, model behavior). Boxes marked show where the current documentation differs from the wording of the guide; on the exam, answer as the guide teaches.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Exam: C C A R F; sixty items; one hundred twenty min; four of six scenarios; pass seven hundred twenty of one thousand; U S D one hundred twenty-five. Domains: D one twenty-seven Agentic, D two eighteen Tools and M C P, D three twenty Claude Code, D four twenty Prompts and structured output, D five fifteen Context and reliability. Task statements: thirty in all: seven, five, six, six, six. Scenarios: Support agent, Claude Code codegen, Multi-agent research, Developer productivity, Claude Code in C I, Structured extraction. Retakes: fourteen, thirty, ninety days; max four per rolling twelve months. Eligibility: Partner Network staff with a company email; Academy courses give completion certificates only. In the next module, we continue the course.
